title: The theory of relativity for everyone
subtitle: Einstein 1905 & 1915
subject: sciences
description: In 1905 and 1915, Einstein changed our idea of space, time and gravity. And without his calculations, your GPS would be off by several kilometers.

hero.hook: Time is not one universal clock. And gravity is not an invisible rope.

blocks.text: In **1905** and **1915**, **Albert Einstein** published two theories that turned physics upside down. Until then, science mostly followed [[Newton]]: time flowed the same way for everyone, everywhere.

Einstein showed that space and time are linked, and that gravity can be understood as a curving of that fabric. These ideas explain [[black holes]] and the [[Big Bang]]. They also correct the GPS in your phone, every single day.

**Special relativity** rests on two simple ideas. The laws of nature are the same for everyone moving at a constant speed. And the speed of light in a vacuum, **about 300,000 km/s**, is the same for everyone, whether you race toward the light or away from it.

blocks.caption: Albert Einstein, author of the theory of relativity

blocks.text: For light to always keep the same speed, time has to give. This is [[time dilation]]: the faster an object moves, the more slowly time passes for it compared with someone at rest. It is not an illusion. **Atomic clocks**, instruments that measure time with extreme precision, have measured it.

From this Einstein also drew [[E=mc²]]: mass is a very concentrated form of energy. Because **c**, the speed of light, is enormous, a tiny amount of mass can release colossal energy. That is one pillar of [[nuclear physics]], the study of atomic nuclei and their reactions.
In 1905, Einstein was not a university professor. He worked as an examiner at the patent office in Bern, Switzerland.

Ten years later, Einstein published **general relativity**. Newton saw gravity as an invisible force pulling masses toward each other. Einstein offered another picture: **spacetime**, space and time joined into a single fabric, behaves like a flexible sheet.

A heavy mass, like the Sun, dents that sheet. Picture a bowling ball on a trampoline. A marble rolled past it does not travel straight: it follows the dip. In the same way, the Earth orbits because it follows the curve the Sun creates.

Even light follows those curves. In **1919**, the British astronomer **Arthur Eddington** checked it during an eclipse: the apparent positions of stars behind the Sun were slightly shifted. Einstein became famous overnight.

sections.title: GPS, the proof in your pocket

blocks.text: GPS satellites circle at about **14,000 km/h**, some **20,000 km** up. To place you within a meter, their clocks have to stay in step with clocks on the ground. But two relativistic effects are at work at once.

Because of their speed, time up there runs a little more slowly, an effect of special relativity: roughly **7 microseconds** lost per day. Because gravity is weaker at that altitude, time up there runs a little faster, an effect of general relativity: roughly **45 microseconds** gained.
Without relativistic corrections, the position error of a GPS could reach about **11 km** a day.
The net result is a gain of about **38 microseconds** a day. That sounds minuscule. At the speed of light, it is already enormous for navigation.

sections.title: Waves, black holes, an expanding universe

blocks.text: General relativity predicts black holes: regions where the curvature is so strong that not even light gets out. Einstein doubted they really existed. Both [[radio astronomy]], the study of the sky in radio waves, and recent images have since confirmed them.

In **1916**, he also predicted **gravitational waves**: ripples in spacetime made by cosmic catastrophes, such as two black holes merging. Detecting them took until **2015** and the **LIGO** observatory, a ground-based detector sensitive to the shivering of space itself.

Finally, these equations opened the way to an expanding universe, the basis of the Big Bang model. Einstein had first added a **cosmological constant**, a mathematical term to force the universe to stand still. Hubble's observations later convinced him otherwise.
**E=mc²** ties mass to energy. General relativity says that gravity curves spacetime. Without those corrections, your GPS would be off by several kilometers every day.
